caption:
A federal judge set a January 20 trial for Abdulrahman Alfozan, the former OpenAI engineering lead accused of hiding a recording device in a conference room.
In court, the prosecutor said he was not aware of evidence of economic espionage, trade secret theft or work as a foreign agent.
The judge gave prosecutors seven days to hand over any such evidence.

paragraphs.text: A federal judge in San Francisco set January 20, 2027 as the trial date for Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineering lead accused of hiding a recording device in a conference room at the company's headquarters, CNBC reported on November 17, 2026. Judge Vince Chhabria of the US District Court in San Francisco is overseeing the case, according to NewsBytes.

Alfozan has pleaded not guilty to one count of intercepting oral communications. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison. Al Jazeera, citing the charging documents, reported that the maximum penalty also includes a fine of up to $250,000.
What the prosecutor told the court

At the hearing, Assistant US Attorney Nick Parker said he was not aware of any evidence that Alfozan committed economic espionage, stole trade secrets or acted as an unregistered agent of a foreign government, according to NewsBytes. CNBC reported that the judge gave prosecutors seven days to disclose any such evidence.

Parker also told the judge that investigators had not been able to get into Alfozan's phone. Prosecutors have collected a second phone, a tablet and two laptops, NewsBytes reported, and they have obtained about 160 hours of recordings from meetings held in the conference room.

The judge ordered prosecutors to give the defense all FBI reports by November 24 and to speed up the delivery of other trial evidence. NewsBytes quoted Chhabria as telling the defense that the court needed to make sure it received the discovery it was entitled to promptly.

According to prosecutors, OpenAI staff found the device wrapped in toilet paper and placed behind a television in the conference room, and surveillance footage shows Alfozan examining it, NewsBytes reported. The FBI arrested Alfozan on October 9, Al Jazeera reported, after prosecutors said he had booked a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for October 12 with his wife and another family member.

Al Jazeera described Alfozan as a 35-year-old Saudi national who joined OpenAI in July 2025 and had previously worked as a systems engineer at Meta. He was also appointed a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a venture capital firm in Riyadh, in February 2025. OpenAI has said it had no proof that he took source code or customer data, according to NewsBytes.

In October, prosecutors persuaded the court to keep Alfozan in custody without bail, arguing that the alleged bugging could endanger US national security, NewsBytes reported. His defense lawyer, David Rizk, has pushed for a quick trial, said the government was slow to share evidence and argued that nothing ties his client to espionage.

The hearing narrows the public picture of the case. Earlier filings focused on the defendant's ties to Saudi Arabia and the risk that he would flee, which led many readers to see it as a possible spying case. For now, the only charge is the interception of private conversations, and the government has a week to show whether it has anything more.
The next marker is the seven-day deadline for prosecutors to disclose any evidence of espionage, trade secret theft or foreign agent activity, followed by the January 20, 2027 trial date.
